caption: PM2.5 7-day rolling mean by day of year, one line per year (top), and the resulting season window per year (bottom). Season onset is defined as the first day the 7-day mean exceeds 37.5 ug/m3.
conclusion: State here whether the window moved between years and by how many days. With only 4 seasons in the record this is a description of what happened, not a basis for forecasting next year's onset.

caption: Days per year exceeding the 37.5 ug/m3 daily standard (left) and monthly mean PM2.5 by year (right).
conclusion: Say explicitly whether the trend is up, down or flat, and whether the record is long enough to call it a trend at all. Four years is not.

caption: Seven-day rolling mean PM2.5 by location (left) and total exceedance days per location (right). Locations returning identical data were removed.
conclusion: Say which places are worse and by how much, and state the caveat: these are neighbouring cells of a ~45 km global model, not independent station measurements, and the model carries no terrain.

caption: Distribution of each meteorological variable on days in the best and worst quartiles of daily mean PM2.5.
conclusion: Name the mechanism, do not just report the correlation: a shallow boundary layer with light wind traps smoke in the basin. The ventilation index (boundary layer height x wind speed) is the compact expression of it.

caption: Mean daily PM2.5 by day of week, split by season. Error bars are one standard error of the mean.
conclusion: If the error bars overlap, say there is no weekly pattern and stop. A weekday effect would point to traffic or industry; its absence points to burning and weather, which do not observe a calendar.

caption: Autocorrelation of daily mean PM2.5 (left) and the distribution of persistence forecast error, split by whether the day crossed the 37.5 threshold (right).
conclusion: Persistence is a strong baseline overall (MAE 4.0) but it is wrong by 10.6 ug/m3 on the 6% of days that cross the standard. Those are the only days a warning system exists for, so that is where a model has to earn its place.

caption: Fire detections within 100 km against PM2.5, at two time scales: one point per day (left, log x-axis) and one point per year (right).
conclusion: At daily scale fires and smoke move together (rho = 0.69). At annual scale they do not: 2024 had the most fires (21,312) and 11 exceedance days, while 2025 had the fewest (9,329) and 29. Year-to-year variation in days over the standard therefore reflects dispersion conditions more than emissions, which makes it the wrong measure to judge burning policy by.
